***Need for Speed*** (***NFS***) is a [racing game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Racing_video_game "Racing video game") franchise published by [Electronic Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronic_Arts "Electronic Arts"). Most entries in the series are generally [arcade racing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arcade_racer "Arcade racer") games centered around illegal [street racing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Street_racing "Street racing"), and task players with completing races of various types while evading police pursuit. Some entries also do not follow the basic setup of most titles and are instead simulation racers, focus on legal circuit races, feature [kart racing game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kart_racing_game "Kart racing game") elements, or feature illegal street racing but do not also feature police pursuits. *Need for Speed* is one of EA's oldest franchises not published under their [EA Sports](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EA_Sports "EA Sports") brand.[[1]](#cite_note-1)

The series' first title, *[The Need for Speed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Need_for_Speed "The Need for Speed")*, was released in 1994. The last installment, *[Need for Speed Unbound](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Need_for_Speed_Unbound "Need for Speed Unbound")*, was released on December 2, 2022. Additionally, a [free-to-play](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free-to-play "Free-to-play") [mobile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mobile_game "Mobile game") installment released in 2015, *[Need for Speed: No Limits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Need_for_Speed:_No_Limits "Need for Speed: No Limits")*, is actively developed by [Firemonkeys Studios](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Firemonkeys_Studios "Firemonkeys Studios") (the developers of *[Real Racing 3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_Racing_3 "Real Racing 3")*).

The series titles have been overseen and developed by multiple notable teams over the years, including [EA Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EA_Canada "EA Canada"), [EA Black Box](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EA_Black_Box "EA Black Box"), [Slightly Mad Studios](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slightly_Mad_Studios "Slightly Mad Studios"), [Criterion Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Criterion_Games "Criterion Games") and [Ghost Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_Games "Ghost Games"). Several *Need for Speed* games have been well-received critically, and the franchise has been one of the [most successful](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_best-selling_video_game_franchises "List of best-selling video game franchises") of all time, selling over 150 million copies as of October 2013.[[2]](#cite_note-2) The [franchise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Media_franchise "Media franchise") has expanded into other forms of media, including a [film adaptation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Need_for_Speed_(film) "Need for Speed (film)") and licensed [Hot Wheels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hot_Wheels "Hot Wheels") toys.[[3]](#cite_note-Alan-3)

## History

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Need_for_Speed&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

The *Need for Speed* series was originally developed by [Distinctive Software](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distinctive_Software "Distinctive Software"), a video game studio based in [Vancouver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vancouver "Vancouver"), [British Columbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Columbia "British Columbia"), Canada. Prior to [Electronic Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronic_Arts "Electronic Arts")' purchase of the company in 1991,[[4]](#cite_note-4) it had created popular racing games such as *[Stunts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stunts_(video_game) "Stunts (video game)")* and *[Test Drive II: The Duel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Test_Drive_II:_The_Duel "Test Drive II: The Duel")*. After the purchase, the company was renamed [Electronic Arts (EA) Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EA_Canada "EA Canada"). The company capitalized on its experience in the domain by developing the *Need for Speed* series in late 1992.[*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*] EA Canada continued to develop and expand the *Need for Speed* franchise up to 2002, when another Vancouver-based developer, named [Black Box Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EA_Black_Box "EA Black Box"), was acquired by EA and contracted to continue the series with *[Need for Speed: Hot Pursuit 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Need_for_Speed:_Hot_Pursuit_2 "Need for Speed: Hot Pursuit 2")*.[[5]](#cite_note-5) Meanwhile, [Slightly Mad Studios](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slightly_Mad_Studios "Slightly Mad Studios") would develop the 2009 [sim racing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sim_racing "Sim racing") title, *[Need for Speed: Shift](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Need_for_Speed:_Shift "Need for Speed: Shift")*, and its 2011 sequel, *[Shift 2: Unleashed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shift_2:_Unleashed "Shift 2: Unleashed")*.

The UK-based [Criterion Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Criterion_Games "Criterion Games") would develop the 2010 *[Hot Pursuit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Need_for_Speed:_Hot_Pursuit_(2010_video_game) "Need for Speed: Hot Pursuit (2010 video game)")* title; a successor to 1998's *[Need for Speed III: Hot Pursuit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Need_for_Speed_III:_Hot_Pursuit "Need for Speed III: Hot Pursuit")*. The game introduced a social platform, titled Autolog, which allows players to track game progress, view leaderboards, share screenshots with friends, among other features.[[6]](#cite_note-6) The 2010 *Hot Pursuit* game would be well-received; a remastered version was released ten years later in 2020.[[7]](#cite_note-polygon-remastered-7) As a result of *Hot Pursuit*'s critical success, in-contrast to the mixed reception of the Black Box-developed installments since 2007's *[Need for Speed: ProStreet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Need_for_Speed:_ProStreet "Need for Speed: ProStreet")*, Criterion would become the lead developer of the franchise going forward.[[8]](#cite_note-8) At [E3 2012](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronic_Entertainment_Expo_2012 "Electronic Entertainment Expo 2012"), Criterion Games vice president Alex Ward announced that random developers would no longer be developing *NFS* titles. Ward wouldn't confirm that all *Need for Speed* games in the future would be developed entirely by Criterion, but he did say the studio would have "strong involvement" in them and would have control over which *NFS* titles would be released in the future.[[9]](#cite_note-Yin-9)[[10]](#cite_note-10)

In August 2013, following the downsizing of Criterion Games, EA Swedish developer [Ghost Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_Games "Ghost Games") would become the main studio for the franchise, and oversee its future development.[[11]](#cite_note-VideoGamer.com-11)[[12]](#cite_note-Scamell-12) At the time, 80% of Ghost Games' work force consisted of former Criterion Games employees.[[11]](#cite_note-VideoGamer.com-11)[[12]](#cite_note-Scamell-12) From 2013 to 2019, Ghost Games would develop *[Need for Speed Rivals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Need_for_Speed_Rivals "Need for Speed Rivals")*, [the 2015](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Need_for_Speed_(2015_video_game) "Need for Speed (2015 video game)") franchise [reboot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reboot_(fiction) "Reboot (fiction)"), 2017's *[Need for Speed Payback](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Need_for_Speed_Payback "Need for Speed Payback")*, and 2019's *[Need for Speed Heat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Need_for_Speed_Heat "Need for Speed Heat")*. While *Rivals* was positively-received, the 2015 reboot and its follow-ups received more mixed reviews.

In February 2020, Criterion regained oversight of the franchise,[[13]](#cite_note-13) with its first release since then being 2022's *[Need for Speed Unbound](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Need_for_Speed_Unbound "Need for Speed Unbound")*. Meanwhile, several past entries (namely *[Need for Speed: Carbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Need_for_Speed:_Carbon "Need for Speed: Carbon")*, *[Need for Speed: Undercover](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Need_for_Speed:_Undercover "Need for Speed: Undercover")*, *Shift*, *Shift 2* and *[Need for Speed: The Run](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Need_for_Speed:_The_Run "Need for Speed: The Run")*), with the exception of 2010's *Hot Pursuit*, and 2012's *[Need for Speed: Most Wanted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Need_for_Speed:_Most_Wanted_(2012_video_game) "Need for Speed: Most Wanted (2012 video game)")*, became delisted from online stores. Their respective online servers were shut down on August 31, 2021.[[14]](#cite_note-14)

As part of a larger company organization in September 2023, Criterion Games was shifted from EA Sports to EA Entertainment, with the majority of the studio working to support the *[Battlefield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battlefield_(video_game_series) "Battlefield (video game series)")* series, though a core group within Criterion continued to work on updates for *Unbound* according to EA's Vince Zampella.[[15]](#cite_note-15) By February 2025, however, the *Need for Speed* franchise was placed on hold as EA shifted the whole of Criterion to work on *[Battlefield 6](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battlefield_6 "Battlefield 6")*, with the studio being later rebranded as Criterion – A Battlefield Studio in August 2025. Whilst EA promised that the series would return in 'new and interesting ways', by July 2026, EA's Rebecka Coutaz confirmed that Criterion would be focused solely on the *Battlefield* series, thus leaving *Need for Speed* with no primary developer.[[16]](#cite_note-16)[[17]](#cite_note-17)[[18]](#cite_note-IGN_July_2026-18)

## Gameplay

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Need_for_Speed&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Gameplay")]

Almost all of the games in the *NFS* series employ the same fundamental rules and similar mechanics: the player controls a [race car](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auto_racing "Auto racing") in a variety of races, the goal being to win the race. In the tournament/career mode, the player must win a series of races to unlock vehicles and tracks. Before each race, the player chooses a vehicle and has the option of selecting either an [automatic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Automatic_transmission "Automatic transmission") or [manual transmission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manual_transmission "Manual transmission"). All games in the series have some form of [multiplayer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multiplayer_video_game "Multiplayer video game") mode allowing players to race one another via a [split screen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Split_screen_(computer_graphics) "Split screen (computer graphics)"), a [LAN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Local_area_network "Local area network") or the Internet. Since *[Need for Speed: High Stakes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Need_for_Speed:_High_Stakes "Need for Speed: High Stakes")*, the series has also integrated [car body customization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modified_car "Modified car") into gameplay.

Although the games share the same name, their tone and focus can vary significantly. For example, in some games the cars can suffer mechanical and visual damage, while in other games the cars cannot be damaged at all; in some games, the software simulates real-car behavior (physics), while in others there are more forgiving physics.

With the release of *[Need for Speed: Underground](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Need_for_Speed:_Underground "Need for Speed: Underground")*, the series shifted from racing [sports cars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_car "Sports car") on scenic point-to-point tracks to an [import/tuner subculture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Import_scene "Import scene") involving [street racing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Street_racing "Street racing") in an urban setting. To date, this theme has remained prevalent in most of the following games.

*[Need for Speed: Shift](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Need_for_Speed:_Shift "Need for Speed: Shift")* and its [sequel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shift_2:_Unleashed "Shift 2: Unleashed") took a [simulator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sim_racing "Sim racing") approach to racing, featuring closed-circuit racing on real tracks like the [Nürburgring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nürburgring "Nürburgring") and [Laguna Seca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laguna_Seca "Laguna Seca"), as well as the fictional street circuits in various cities like [London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London "London") and [Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago "Chicago"). The car lists include a combination of exotics, sports cars, and tuners in addition to special race cars.

Most of the games in the franchise include [police pursuits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Car_chase "Car chase") in some form or other. In some of the games featuring police pursuit (e.g. *[Need for Speed III: Hot Pursuit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Need_for_Speed_III:_Hot_Pursuit "Need for Speed III: Hot Pursuit")*), the player can play as either the felon or the cop.[[19]](#cite_note-19) The concepts of [drifting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drifting_(motorsport) "Drifting (motorsport)") and [dragging](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drag_racing "Drag racing") were introduced in *Need for Speed: Underground*. These new mechanics are included in the tournament/career mode aside from the regular street races. In drift races, in games like *Underground* and *[Need for Speed (2015)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Need_for_Speed_(2015_video_game) "Need for Speed (2015 video game)")*, the player must defeat other racers by totaling the most points, earned by the length and timing of the drift made by the player's vehicle.[[20]](#cite_note-Draftdriftdrag-20) In drag races, the player must finish first to win the race, though if the player crashes into an obstacle or wall, the race ends.[[20]](#cite_note-Draftdriftdrag-20) In *[Need for Speed Payback](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Need_for_Speed_Payback "Need for Speed Payback")*, the player has to earn a certain number of points to win; increase their multiplier based on how many points they get, whilst passing through a limited number of checkpoints.[[21]](#cite_note-21)

The concept of [car tuning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Car_tuning "Car tuning") evolved with each new game, from focusing mainly on the mechanics of the car to including how the car looks. Each game except *[Need for Speed: Hot Pursuit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Need_for_Speed:_Hot_Pursuit_(2010_video_game) "Need for Speed: Hot Pursuit (2010 video game)")* has car tuning which can set options for items like [ABS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-lock_braking_system "Anti-lock braking system"), [traction control](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Traction_control_system "Traction control system"), or [downforce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Downforce#Front "Downforce"), or for upgrading parts like the engine or gearbox. Visual tuning of the player's car becomes important in tournament/career mode after the release of *[Need for Speed: Underground 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Need_for_Speed:_Underground_2 "Need for Speed: Underground 2")*, when the appearance is rated from zero to ten points. When a car attains a high enough visual rating, the vehicle is eligible to be on the cover of a fictional magazine.[[22]](#cite_note-22)

Like all racing games, the *Need for Speed* series features a list of cars, modeled and named after actual cars. Cars in the franchise are divided into four categories: [exotic cars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supercar "Supercar"), [muscle cars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muscle_car "Muscle car"), [tuners](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Car_tuning "Car tuning"), and special vehicles.[[23]](#cite_note-cars-23) Exotic cars feature high performance, expensive cars like the [Lamborghini Murciélago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lamborghini_Murciélago "Lamborghini Murciélago"), [Mercedes-Benz SLR McLaren](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercedes-Benz_SLR_McLaren "Mercedes-Benz SLR McLaren"), [Chevrolet Corvette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chevrolet_Corvette "Chevrolet Corvette") and the [Ford GT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ford_GT "Ford GT"); muscle cars refer to the [Ford Mustang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ford_Mustang "Ford Mustang"), [Dodge Challenger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dodge_Challenger "Dodge Challenger") and the [Chevrolet Camaro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chevrolet_Camaro "Chevrolet Camaro"); while tuner cars are cars like the [Nissan Skyline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nissan_Skyline "Nissan Skyline") and the [Mitsubishi Lancer Evolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mitsubishi_Lancer_Evolution "Mitsubishi Lancer Evolution"). The special vehicles are civilian and police cars that are available for use in some games, such as the [Ford Crown Victoria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ford_Crown_Victoria "Ford Crown Victoria") in *Need for Speed: Hot Pursuit* and garbage trucks, fire engines and taxis in *[Need for Speed: Carbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Need_for_Speed:_Carbon "Need for Speed: Carbon")*.[[23]](#cite_note-cars-23)

Originally the series took place in international settings, such as [race tracks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Race_track "Race track") in [Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australia "Australia"), [Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europe "Europe"), and [Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Africa "Africa").[[24]](#cite_note-24) Beginning with *Underground*, the series has taken place in fictional [metropolitan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_area "Metropolitan area") cities.[[25]](#cite_note-UG1-25) The first game featured [traffic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Traffic "Traffic") on "head to head" mode, while later games traffic can be toggled on and off, and starting with *Underground*, traffic is a fixed obstacle.[[25]](#cite_note-UG1-25) Most of the recent *Need for Speed* games are set in fictional locations of our world, in a number of different time periods. These include, but are not limited to, Olympic, Bayview, Rockport, Palmont City, Tri-City Bay, Seacrest County, Fairhaven City, Redview County, Ventura Bay, Fortune Valley, Palm City and Lakeshore City.

#### *The Need for Speed* (1994)

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Need_for_Speed&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: The Need for Speed (1994)")]

Main article: [*The Need for Speed*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Need_for_Speed "The Need for Speed")

The original *Need for Speed* was released for [3DO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3DO_Interactive_Multiplayer "3DO Interactive Multiplayer") in 1994 with versions released for [MS-DOS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MS-DOS "MS-DOS") (1995), [PlayStation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PlayStation_(console) "PlayStation (console)"), and [Saturn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sega_Saturn "Sega Saturn") (1996) following shortly afterwards. *The Need for Speed* and its *Special Edition* were the only games in the series to support DOS, with subsequent releases for the PC running only on Windows (excluding *Need for Speed: Carbon* which was also released on Mac OS X).

The first installment of *The Need for Speed* was the only serious attempt by the series to provide a realistic simulation of car handling elements through the direct collaboration of Staff members from *[Road & Track](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Road_&_Track "Road & Track")*. Electronic Arts left the handling dynamics tuning with the automotive magazine's seasoned drivers to match vehicle behavior including realistic over and understeer that remains impressive decades later, as well as sounds made by the vehicles' gear control levers and other functions. The game contained vehicle data with spoken commentary, several "magazine-style" images of each car, and short video clips highlighting the vehicles set to music. Most cars and tracks are available at the beginning of the game, and the objective is to unlock the remaining locked content by winning tournaments. This version featured chases by police cars, a popular theme throughout the series.

Another version called *The Need for Speed: Special Edition*, was released only for the PC in 1996. It featured support for [DirectX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DirectX "DirectX") 2 and [TCP/IP networking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internet_protocol_suite "Internet protocol suite"), two new tracks, but dropped the ever-popular flip and go in favor of the more generic scene reset after an accident, a portents of the arcade-style gaming that would dominate the series ever after.

#### *Need for Speed II* (1997)

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Need_for_Speed&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Need for Speed II (1997)")]

Main article: [*Need for Speed II*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Need_for_Speed_II "Need for Speed II")

*Need for Speed II* (*NFS II*) featured some rare and exotic vehicles, including the [Ford Indigo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ford_Indigo "Ford Indigo") concept vehicle, and featured country-themed tracks from North America, Europe, Asia, and Australia. A new racing mode was also introduced, dubbed "Knockout", where the last racers to finish laps will be eliminated. In addition, track design was more open-ended; players could now "drive" off the asphalt, and cut across fields to take advantage of shortcuts. *Need for Speed II: Special Edition* includes one extra track, extra cars, and support for [Glide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glide_API "Glide API"). The PlayStation port of *NFS II* also took advantage of the [NeGcon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NeGcon "NeGcon") controller, and the [Dual Analog](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dual_Analog_Controller "Dual Analog Controller") and [DualShock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DualShock "DualShock") controllers as well.

#### *Need for Speed III: Hot Pursuit* (1998)

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Need_for_Speed&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Need for Speed III: Hot Pursuit (1998)")]

Main article: [*Need for Speed III: Hot Pursuit*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Need_for_Speed_III:_Hot_Pursuit "Need for Speed III: Hot Pursuit")

*Need for Speed III: Hot Pursuit* added *Hot Pursuit* mode, where the player either attempted to outrun the police or be the cop, arresting speeders. *NFS III* took advantage of the multimedia capabilities by featuring audio commentary, picture slideshows, and music videos. This game was the first in the series to allow the downloading of additional cars from the official website. As a result, [modding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mod_(video_gaming) "Mod (video gaming)") communities sprang up to create vehicles. The PC version was also the first game in the series to support Direct3D hardware.

#### *Need for Speed: High Stakes* (1999)

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Need_for_Speed&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Need for Speed: High Stakes (1999)")]

Main article: [*Need for Speed: High Stakes*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Need_for_Speed:_High_Stakes "Need for Speed: High Stakes")

*High Stakes*, developed by EA Canada and EA Seattle, was released in 1999. The game features more realistic elements than its predecessors and introduced a damage system that allows cars to take damage when colliding with objects, affecting their appearance and performance. It also introduced a series of economy-based tournaments, awarding players with a cash prize that can be spent on repairing, purchasing, or upgrading cars for subsequent races. The game's Hot Pursuit mode, which was introduced in *Hot Pursuit*, was expanded with more options, allowing players to control police pursuits attempting to stop racers.

#### *Need for Speed: Porsche Unleashed* (2000)

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Need_for_Speed&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Need for Speed: Porsche Unleashed (2000)")]

Main article: [*Need for Speed: Porsche Unleashed*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Need_for_Speed:_Porsche_Unleashed "Need for Speed: Porsche Unleashed")

*Porsche Unleashed* (North America and Latin America title), *Porsche 2000* (European and Australian title), or simply *Porsche* (in Germany) is different from the previous versions because it featured only [Porsches](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Porsche "Porsche").

The vehicle handling in the PC version was said to be the most realistic in any *NFS* game, but the PSX (PS1) version had very simplified arcade handling that fell woefully short of the hallmark handling offered in the first game. The player had to win races to unlock cars in chronological order from 1950 to 2000. *Porsche Unleashed* also featured a Factory Driver mode, where the player had to test Porsches to move forward in the game and did not feature a split-screen mode.

#### *Need for Speed: Hot Pursuit 2* (2002)

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Need_for_Speed&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Need for Speed: Hot Pursuit 2 (2002)")]

Main article: [*Need for Speed: Hot Pursuit 2*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Need_for_Speed:_Hot_Pursuit_2 "Need for Speed: Hot Pursuit 2")

*Need for Speed: Hot Pursuit 2* was the debut NFS title from [EA Black Box](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EA_Canada "EA Canada"), and the first *NFS* for the [sixth generation consoles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_video_game_consoles_(sixth_generation) "History of video game consoles (sixth generation)"). Different versions of the game were produced for each platform. The [Xbox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xbox_(console) "Xbox (console)"), [GameCube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GameCube "GameCube"), and [Microsoft Windows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microsoft_Windows "Microsoft Windows") versions were developed by EA Seattle, while the PS2 version was developed by Black Box Games in Vancouver.

*Hot Pursuit 2* draws primarily from the gameplay and style of *NFS III*, putting emphasis on evading the police and over-the-top tracks. Although the game allowed players to play as the police, the pursuit mode was less realistic than preceding versions of *NFS*; players merely needed to "tap" a speeder to arrest them, as opposed to using simulated police tactics to immobilize a speeding vehicle. This was the first version since the start of the series not to feature an "in the driving seat" (cockpit) camera view, transitioning EA from realistic racing to arcade street racing. It was the last game in the series for the PC version to feature the split-screen two-player mode introduced in *Need for Speed II*. For the multiplayer mode of the PC version, [GameSpy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GameSpy "GameSpy")'s internet matchmaking system was used in place of Local Area Network (LAN) play. *Hot Pursuit 2* was the first *NFS* game to use songs sung by licensed artists under the EA Trax label.

#### *Need for Speed: Underground* (2003)

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Need_for_Speed&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Need for Speed: Underground (2003)")]

Main article: [*Need for Speed: Underground*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Need_for_Speed:_Underground "Need for Speed: Underground")

*Need for Speed: Underground* was developed by EA Black Box and released in 2003. On PC, this was the first *NFS* game to require Hardware Transform and Lighting in graphics cards. Most of the new elements in *Underground* became defining marks of later installments in the *Need for Speed* series.

*Underground* shifted from semi-professional racing and isolated circuits to the [street racing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Street_racing "Street racing") style of other [arcade racing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Racing_video_game "Racing video game") series: all circuits became part of a single map, Olympic City, except for drifts. *Underground* introduced two new play modes (Drag and Drift) and more tuning options than in the earlier *[High Stakes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Need_for_Speed:_High_Stakes "Need for Speed: High Stakes")*. *Underground* was also the first game in the series to feature a story, told via [pre-rendered](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pre-rendering "Pre-rendering") videos. *Underground* features tuner cars and has a wide variety of tuning options such as widebody kits, bumpers, spoilers, as well as performance upgrades such as engines and [nitrous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrous_oxide "Nitrous oxide"). City street racing is the primary focus of the game. There are no police in *Underground* and *Underground 2*, which drew criticism as police had been an important part of previous titles.

#### *Need for Speed: Underground 2* (2004)

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Need_for_Speed&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Need for Speed: Underground 2 (2004)")]

Main article: [*Need for Speed: Underground 2*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Need_for_Speed:_Underground_2 "Need for Speed: Underground 2")

*Need for Speed: Underground 2*, was developed by EA Black Box and released in 2004. A demo of the game was placed as a bonus in copies of the EA/[Criterion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Criterion_Games "Criterion Games") collaboration *[Burnout 3: Takedown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burnout_3:_Takedown "Burnout 3: Takedown")*.

In *Underground 2*, the story mode continued, but there were new racing modes such as Underground Racing League and Street X, more tuning options, and a new method of selecting races. Also included was an "outrun" mode where a player can challenge random opponents on the road (similar to *[Tokyo Xtreme Racer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tokyo_Xtreme_Racer "Tokyo Xtreme Racer")*). *Underground 2* also introduced several [SUVs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sport_utility_vehicle "Sport utility vehicle"), used to race against other SUVs. The most significant change vs. the original *Underground* was the introduction of its open world (free roam) environments,[[127]](#cite_note-128) setting the tone for numerous NFS games to come. This was also the publisher's most marketed feature at launch. In addition, the game featured actresses/models [Brooke Burke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brooke_Burke "Brooke Burke") and [Kelly Brook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kelly_Brook "Kelly Brook") as in-game characters to help guide the player through the campaign.[[128]](#cite_note-129)

The customization features were significantly expanded on modifications that did not affect vehicle performance. Players were required to customize their car to a certain numerical value in order to be offered DVD and magazine covers, the only way to advance to higher game levels. The game featured more extensive [product placement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Product_placement "Product placement") for companies with no connection to auto racing. This game also had extensive customization options in the form of suspension upgrades, nitrous systems, and engine mods.

*Need for Speed: Underground Rivals* was the first *Need for Speed* game released on the PlayStation Portable. Different from *Need for Speed: Underground 2* as it had no free roam and the cars were very limited, it was released in 2005.

#### *Need for Speed: Most Wanted* (2005)

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Need_for_Speed&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Need for Speed: Most Wanted (2005)")]

Main article: [*Need for Speed: Most Wanted* (2005 video game)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Need_for_Speed:_Most_Wanted_(2005_video_game) "Need for Speed: Most Wanted (2005 video game)")

*Need for Speed: Most Wanted* was developed by EA Black Box, released in 2005, and was one of the first games released for the [Xbox 360](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xbox_360 "Xbox 360"). The [PlayStation Portable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PlayStation_Portable "PlayStation Portable") port of *Most Wanted* is titled *[Need for Speed: Most Wanted 5-1-0](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Need_for_Speed:_Most_Wanted_(2005_video_game)#Development_and_release "Need for Speed: Most Wanted (2005 video game)")*.

Police chases represent a significant body of the gameplay, and includes the [free-roaming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_world "Open world") aspect of *Underground 2*, but with less extensive vehicle customization features. The story mode is a different style from *Underground*, with CGI effects mixed with live-action. The game featured the Blacklist, a crew consisting of 15 racers that the player must beat one-by-one to unlock parts, cars, tracks, and to complete career mode. The player had to meet certain requirements before they could take on the next Blacklist rival, such as races completed, milestones achieved, and bounty earned.

A special *Black Edition* of *Most Wanted* was also released, featuring additional races, challenges, and a few bonus cars; it also included a behind-the-scenes [DVD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DVD "DVD"). Both versions were available for the PlayStation 2, Xbox, and Windows-based PCs, while only the standard edition was available for GameCube, Nintendo DS, and Xbox 360.

*Most Wanted* had extremely positive reviews and received universal acclaim from reviewers in many gaming websites and magazines, praising the graphics, sound effects, and general gameplay. With 16 million copies sold worldwide, *Most Wanted* is the best-selling game in the franchise.[[129]](#cite_note-130) A game, also named *[Need for Speed: Most Wanted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Need_for_Speed:_Most_Wanted_(2012_video_game) "Need for Speed: Most Wanted (2012 video game)")*, was released in 2012 with British developer [Criterion Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Criterion_Games "Criterion Games") responsible for the development.

#### *Need for Speed: Carbon* (2006)

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Need_for_Speed&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Need for Speed: Carbon (2006)")]

Main article: [*Need for Speed: Carbon*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Need_for_Speed:_Carbon "Need for Speed: Carbon")

*Need for Speed: Carbon* was developed by EA Black Box in 2006. It was the first *NFS* game for the [PlayStation 3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PlayStation_3 "PlayStation 3") and the [Wii](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii "Wii") and the last *NFS* game for the [GameCube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GameCube "GameCube"), the [Game Boy Advance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_Boy_Advance "Game Boy Advance"), and the [Xbox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xbox_(console) "Xbox (console)"). *Carbon's* handheld port is known as *[Need for Speed: Carbon – Own the City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Need_for_Speed:_Carbon "Need for Speed: Carbon")*. The Wii port lacked online but made full use of the [Wii Remote](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii_Remote "Wii Remote") and Nunchuk.

*NFS: Carbon* continued the story from *[Most Wanted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Need_for_Speed:_Most_Wanted_(2005_video_game) "Need for Speed: Most Wanted (2005 video game)")*, but the game has far less emphasis on the police. *Carbon* saw the return of nighttime-only racing, with a selection of cars similar to that of *Most Wanted*. *Carbon* introduced a new feature wherein the player is allowed to form a "[crew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crew "Crew")" that aids the player in races. Drift events returned to the series in *Carbon*. Drag racing was removed from the series, but a new type of race called "Canyon Duel" was added, where the closer the player is to the leader, the more points they accrue. If the player overtakes the leader and remains in front for 10 seconds, they win automatically. Another new feature is "Autosculpt", which allows players to custom-fabricate their own auto parts.

The Collector's Edition features three new cars, ten specially tuned cars, six new races, and a bonus DVD with behind-the-scenes footage on the making of the game.

Main article: [*Need for Speed: Undercover*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Need_for_Speed:_Undercover "Need for Speed: Undercover")

*Need for Speed: Undercover*, developed by EA Black Box, was released in 2008. The game had a significantly longer development cycle than previous games, taking 16 months to develop.[[132]](#cite_note-Riccitiello-133) EA ported *Undercover* to various mobile devices. It was the last *Need for Speed* game for [PlayStation 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PlayStation_2 "PlayStation 2"). EA Games president Frank Gibeau stated that since sales of *ProStreet* did not live up to EA's projections, the franchise would go back to its "roots". However, the game received lower scores on aggregate than *ProStreet*.

The game focused on tuning and police chases, featured over 50 cars, and took place in a fictional city called Tri-City Bay. The player's role was as an undercover cop, trying to stop street racers. Containing live-action cutscenes that feature the actress [Maggie Q](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maggie_Q "Maggie Q"), the game also featured a damage system where parts could break off after a crash.

The *Collector's Edition* for PlayStation 3 and Xbox 360 added another five new cars, twelve new circuits, and sprint and checkpoint track configurations. Also included were specially tuned versions of ten existing cars, plus 35 exclusive vinyls for adding a unique visual style.

#### *Need for Speed: Shift* (2009)

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Need_for_Speed&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Need for Speed: Shift (2009)")]

Main article: [*Need for Speed: Shift*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Need_for_Speed:_Shift "Need for Speed: Shift")

*Need for Speed: Shift*, developed by Slightly Mad Studios, was released in 2009. It features over 60 cars and 19 tracks, some of which are licensed tracks while others are fictional. The improved driving simulation was accompanied by an adaptive difficulty, while it reintroduced a cockpit view. *NFS: Shift* focused on racing simulation rather than the arcade racing of previous titles.

*NFS: Shift* received better reviews than the prior three games in the series. The *Special Edition* contained a specially-tuned BMW M3 GT2, and an Elite Series track. Two items of downloadable content were released for the game.

*Need for Speed: Nitro-X* (2010) is a newer installment for use with the [DSi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DSi "Nintendo DSi")/[XL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DSi_XL "Nintendo DSi XL") and the [3DS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_3DS "Nintendo 3DS") system. It took on the gameplay style of *Most Wanted* and *Carbon*, focusing on illegal street racing, tuning and police chases, and adding classic MMO elements to the mix. *World* incorporated almost exact replicas of the cities of Rockport and Palmont, the cities of *Most Wanted* and *Carbon* respectively, into its map design. *World* was originally scheduled for an Asian release in the summer of 2009, but the game was not released at that time and it was released worldwide in 2010.[[134]](#cite_note-nfs-blog-timeline-135)[[135]](#cite_note-EG1-136) The game was in public beta-testing limited to residents of Taiwan in October 2009

Promotion of *[Need for Speed: Hot Pursuit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Need_for_Speed:_Hot_Pursuit_(2010_video_game) "Need for Speed: Hot Pursuit (2010 video game)")* at [Gamescom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gamescom "Gamescom") 2010

*Need for Speed: Hot Pursuit* was developed by British games developer Criterion Games and published by Electronic Arts in 2010.[[137]](#cite_note-Joystiq-138) It focuses on racing and police chases rather than car customization. The game won many awards at the E3 2010, including "Best Racing Game", becoming the first game in the *NFS* series since the original *Hot Pursuit* to win an [E3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronic_Entertainment_Expo "Electronic Entertainment Expo") award.

There were over 60 cars, most available to both racers and cops, but a few were exclusive to either side.[[138]](#cite_note-interview1-139) Unlike previous *NFS* titles, there was no customization, and the game takes place in a fictional rural area called Seacrest County, which the "free roam" feature lets you explore. *Hot Pursuit* allows play as either police or racer. The game also features many weapons, with some exclusive to the cops or racers. The biggest feature introduced was Autolog, which tracked player progressions and recommended events to play. In addition to its statistical system, Autolog also features [Facebook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Facebook "Facebook")-like speedwalls where players can post their comments and photos while in the game. *Hot Pursuit* has received some of the best reviews of the series.

The *Limited Edition* gives players exclusive access to the [Alfa Romeo 8C Competizione](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfa_Romeo_8C_Competizione "Alfa Romeo 8C Competizione") and Ford [Shelby GT500](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shelby_GT500 "Shelby GT500"). Various downloadable content was released for the game.

A remastered version of the game, *Need for Speed: Hot Pursuit Remastered*, was released in November 2020 for [PlayStation 4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PlayStation_4 "PlayStation 4"), [Xbox One](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xbox_One "Xbox One"), [Nintendo Switch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_Switch "Nintendo Switch"), and Microsoft Windows.[[139]](#cite_note-polygon-nfshpr-140) It features cross-platform multiplayer, enhanced visuals, quality-of-life improvements, all main DLC from the PlayStation 3 and Xbox 360 versions, the return of Autolog, and 4K support for PlayStation 4 Pro, Xbox One X, and Windows.[[139]](#cite_note-polygon-nfshpr-140)

*Need for Speed: The Run* was developed by EA Black Box, and released in 2011. The game continued the street-racing gameplay of Black Box's previous titles, with a story based on a race across the United States from San Francisco to New York.

The game featured [quick time events](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quick_time_event "Quick time event") with the player, for the first time in *NFS* history, exiting their car and traveling on foot. *The Run* was powered by [DICE](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EA_Digital_Illusions_CE "EA Digital Illusions CE")'s [Frostbite 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frostbite_(game_engine) "Frostbite (game engine)") [engine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_engine "Game engine"), making the game the first non-shooter and one of the first console titles to use the engine. Additionally, the *NFS* [Autolog](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autolog "Autolog") was also used in the game.

*The Run* employs a large range of real-world vehicles, which can be altered with visual upgrades. An XP (Experience points) system is used for unlocking cars and events. The *Limited Edition* features three exclusive cars and five exclusive challenges with bonus rewards and achievements.

The game picked up on the *[Most Wanted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Need_for_Speed:_Most_Wanted_(2005_video_game) "Need for Speed: Most Wanted (2005 video game)")* IP, as opposed to the *[Hot Pursuit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Need_for_Speed:_Hot_Pursuit_(2010_video_game) "Need for Speed: Hot Pursuit (2010 video game)")* extension.[[142]](#cite_note-143) This was the first game made subsequent to Criterion Games taking over the *NFS* series from Black Box.

#### *Need for Speed: Most Wanted 5-1-0* (2005)

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Need_for_Speed&action=edit&section=37 "Edit section: Need for Speed: Most Wanted 5-1-0 (2005)")]

*Need for Speed: Most Wanted 5-1-0* is a [PlayStation Portable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PlayStation_Portable "PlayStation Portable") spin-off of *Most Wanted*, released on the same day as its console and PC counterpart. Similar to *Most Wanted*, *Most Wanted 5-1-0* features a similar 15-number blacklist and Career mode, with the addition of Tuner Takedown, a "Be the Cop" mode not found in *Most Wanted*. *Most Wanted 5-1-0* lacks many elements of its console and PC counterparts, such as cutscenes, a storyline, and a free-roam mode, and contains minor differences (including the inclusion of a blacklist racer's real name instead of their nickname). The game's title is based on the numbers 5-1-0, which is the police code for street racing.

#### *Need for Speed Mobile* (2024)

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Need_for_Speed&action=edit&section=38 "Edit section: Need for Speed Mobile (2024)")]

*Need for Speed Mobile* (known as *Need for Speed: Assemble* in China, Taiwan, Hong Kong and Macau) is a [free-to-play](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free-to-play "Free-to-play") [Open world](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_world "Open world") [racing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Racing "Racing") [mobile game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mobile_game "Mobile game") developed by [TiMi Studios](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TiMi_Studios "TiMi Studios") and published by [Electronic Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronic_Arts "Electronic Arts") for worldwide and [Tencent Interactive Entertainment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tencent "Tencent") for China and [Garena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garena "Garena") for Taiwan, Hong Kong and Macau.[[158]](#cite_note-159) The game runs on the [Unreal Engine 4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unreal_Engine_4 "Unreal Engine 4"), this is the first and also only game which runs on Unreal Engine in the series. The game released on July 11, 2024 in China,[[159]](#cite_note-160) and released on October 31, 2024 in Taiwan, Hong Kong and Macau.[[160]](#cite_note-161)

### Cancelled games

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Need_for_Speed&action=edit&section=39 "Edit section: Cancelled games")]

#### *Need for Speed 64* (canceled)

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Need_for_Speed&action=edit&section=40 "Edit section: Need for Speed 64 (canceled)")]

In the late 1990s, EA Canada partnered with [Paradigm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paradigm_Entertainment "Paradigm Entertainment") to work on an entry in the series for the [Nintendo 64](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_64 "Nintendo 64"). It was described in the *Next Generation* magazine as having exclusive tracks and vehicles, Rumble Pak support and the series' trademark gameplay mechanics.[[161]](#cite_note-NGen_46-162) The game was ultimately canceled between late 1998 and early 1999. Electronic Arts had signed a deal with Volkswagen to make a game around the [New Beetle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Beetle "New Beetle"), thus altering the *Need for Speed 64* project into *[Beetle Adventure Racing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beetle_Adventure_Racing "Beetle Adventure Racing")*.[[162]](#cite_note-NGen_53-163)

#### *Need for Speed: Ferrari* (canceled)

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Need_for_Speed&action=edit&section=41 "Edit section: Need for Speed: Ferrari (canceled)")]

At the time of the beginning of the development of *Porsche Unleashed*, Electronic Arts was planning to make similar games with Ferrari and BMW. Because EA Canada would develop *Porsche Unleashed*, EA Seattle was counting on developing the Ferrari game, although this idea was canceled even before the release of *Porsche Unleashed*.[[163]](#cite_note-164)

#### *Need for Speed 10: TerrorFive* (canceled)

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Need_for_Speed&action=edit&section=42 "Edit section: Need for Speed 10: TerrorFive (canceled)")]

*Need for Speed 10: TerrorFive* was a concept pitched to Electronic Arts around 2008. The portfolio page of a former presentation director of EA Black Box says the "goal" of the game was to answer the question "How can large scale street races take place in a post 911 US city?" Concept art depicts a group of street racers named "TerrorFive", alongside a mockup of gameplay in which players seemingly hack into police cars.[[164]](#cite_note-165)[[165]](#cite_note-166)[[166]](#cite_note-167)

#### *Need for Speed: Millionaire* (canceled)

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Need_for_Speed&action=edit&section=43 "Edit section: Need for Speed: Millionaire (canceled)")]

*Need for Speed: Millionaire* was a canceled online-only entry developed by Criterion Games, which started development around 2008 after the release of *Burnout Paradise* and *Need For Speed: Undercover*. It would have seen the player and friends go on adventures after a lottery win and the purchase of many supercars, described by Criterion director Alex Ward as "Freeburn meets [Top Gear challenges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Top_Gear_challenges "Top Gear challenges")". The game was worked on for six months and had a playable version, but was canceled in favor of *Need for Speed: Hot Pursuit*.[[167]](#cite_note-168)[[168]](#cite_note-169)

#### *Need for Speed: Edge* (canceled)

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Need_for_Speed&action=edit&section=44 "Edit section: Need for Speed: Edge (canceled)")]

*Need for Speed: Edge* was a [free-to-play](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free-to-play "Free-to-play") [MMO racing game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massively_multiplayer_online_racing_game "Massively multiplayer online racing game") developed by EA Spearhead (formerly EA Korea) and published by Nexon from South Korea and [Tencent Interactive Entertainment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tencent "Tencent") (known as *Need for Speed Online*) from China. It is the third free-to-play game in the franchise overall, along with being the only free-to-play racing game that runs on the [Frostbite 3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frostbite_(game_engine) "Frostbite (game engine)") game engine. The PC version is based on the 2013 title *[Need for Speed Rivals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Need_for_Speed_Rivals "Need for Speed Rivals")*, while the mobile version (sometimes referred to as *Need for Speed: Duel*) is based on *Need for Speed: No Limits*.[[169]](#cite_note-170) Released on December 14, 2017.[[170]](#cite_note-171) Nexon shut down the game on May 30, 2019.[[171]](#cite_note-172)

## Film adaptation

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Need_for_Speed&action=edit&section=45 "Edit section: Film adaptation")]

Main article: [*Need for Speed* (film)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Need_for_Speed_(film) "Need for Speed (film)")

EA worked with [DreamWorks Pictures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DreamWorks_Pictures "DreamWorks Pictures") to create a film version of *[Need for Speed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Need_for_Speed_(film) "Need for Speed (film)")* starring [Aaron Paul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Paul "Aaron Paul") as Tobey Marshall, a mechanic and street racer who was framed by a wealthy business associate.[[172]](#cite_note-173)[[173]](#cite_note-174) The movie was released by [Disney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Walt_Disney_Company "The Walt Disney Company")'s [Touchstone Pictures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Touchstone_Pictures "Touchstone Pictures") on March 14, 2014, months before the franchise's 20th anniversary. Despite receiving negative reviews, the film ended up grossing over $200 million at the worldwide box office.

In April 2015, a sequel was reported to be produced by [China Movie Channel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Movie_Channel "China Movie Channel"), Jiaflix, and 1905.com in association with EA Games.[[174]](#cite_note-175)[[175]](#cite_note-176)
